newsitem.title: USA: Romania, eager to join NATO, touts economic plan.
newsitem.headline: Romania, eager to join NATO, touts economic plan.

text.p: Romania on Tuesday touted the benefits of its economic shock therapy program in a bid to attract international financial support and burnish its credentials as a potential future member of NATO.

Visiting Finance Minister Mircea Ciumara told a small group of reporters that the ambitious reform program is designed to break the back of inflation and dramatically reduce the role of government in the economy.
"We are going to privatize 50 companies per week," Ciumara, speaking through an interpreter, said.
He said he expects the International Monetary Fund to approve a $400 million, one-year stand-by loan to back up Romania's reforms at a board meeting in mid-April.
The World Bank is slated to kick in about another $600 million for worker retraining and support for farmers.

Both the Bank and the IMF witheld funds from Romania last year because the former leftist government failed to live up to its promises to reform the economy. That government was defeated in elections last November by a centrist coalition led by Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea.

Ciumara said that the tough reforms have the backing of the Romanian people even though the measures have already led to higher inflation and unemployment as prices have been freed from government control and state-run firms been shut down.
Romanian Ambassador to the United States Mircea Geoana said the country's citizens recognize that the alternative could be economic chaos similar to that now confronting Bulgaria.
They also realize that Romania's economy is one of the weakest points in the ex-communist nation's bid to gain quick admission to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, he said.

Romania is lobbying for support for first-wave admission to NATO, alongside more developed east Europeans Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, viewed as near-certain entrants to the military alliance.
Ciumara said that Romania plans to change about 80 laws in the next month alone, with many of the measures aimed at making it easier to invest in Romania.
He expects several billion dollars worth of foreign direct investment in the country in the second half of this year, including some major contracts with U.S. companies.
Prime candidates for foreign investment include the telecommunications, aviation, energy, agriculture and petrochemical industries.

Romania also plans to borrow up to $3.2 billion from international capital markets this year. In a shift of policy, the borrowing will be carried out directly by the Finance Ministry, rather than via the central bank.
